name: Nora Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the woodwinds in a small civic orchestra, play oboe solos and teach oboe and beginner clarinet at the arts centre. My music master's helps me coach a section through difficult entrances, but the town contract pays less than that responsibility deserves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does that mean for life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Luis does delivery shifts, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about two weeks of expenses saved and few other oboe posts nearby. I use AI every day to draft rehearsal notes and sort bookings, then I check the music and dates myself.

say: I'd ask for **paid rehearsal time** before celebrating faster messages.
I'd tell players a **tidy calendar** cannot cover a cancelled fee.
think: Our **two-week reserve** and variable delivery shifts leave little room for a missed concert.
I use **AI daily** for draft notices, then check each date against the signed schedule.
do: Get **two concert dates** signed and confirm five paid pupils for next term.
Pause the children's **paid swim club** for a month if a concert is cancelled.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one missing live fee could disrupt essential bills.
S0.quote: The players do not owe their evening to a guessed call time.
fieldNote: Her **senior musical role** sits on low pay and a two-week reserve, making cancellation costly.
Her **daily AI use** is checked against signed rehearsal times rather than trusted blindly.

steps.text: Get two concert dates signed and confirm five paid pupils
Pause paid swim club for a month if concert fee is cancelled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the players that faster booking notes are pleasant, but the centre still needs to pay for rehearsal. A tidy calendar cannot cover a cancelled fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays small, the oboe chair remains, but our low pay and two-week reserve already make a cancelled concert hard. Luis's delivery shifts vary, so I cannot call the household secure just because the software disappoints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask for signed dates for the next two concerts and confirm my five paid arts-centre pupils for next term. If a concert is cancelled, we'll pause the children's paid swim club for that month and keep the mortgage current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even with little AI change. One missing live fee would reach the household before the next delivery payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a cancellation already affected a bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A concert was cancelled in May after the programme was printed. The centre paid nothing for the cancelled performance or our preparation, and Luis took extra weekend deliveries to cover the electricity bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a draft rehearsal notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI for draft rehearsal notices, but I compare every time with the conductor's signed schedule. The players do not owe their evening to a guessed call time.

say: I'd ask for **written preparation fees** before accepting a new centre contract.
I'd bring **invoice evidence** to the players and association.
think: Nearly **one-third of my pay** from arrangements and notes may shrink.
Two weeks saved makes a **third-pay gap** an immediate mortgage risk.
do: Compare **ten invoices** with new centre hours and bring evidence to the association this month.
Trial a new **AI cleanup tool** only on owned takes with paid-use licence and manual note checks.
Require **written player permission** for other recordings; stop if notes appear falsely or someone's line disappears.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because likely lost fees exceed our thin savings.
S1.quote: Fast audio cleanup does not restore my paid arranging hours.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI habit** does not protect the paid arrangement hours that clients may stop buying.
Her **new audio trial** preserves ownership, licence, written consent and note-by-note manual checks.

steps.text: Bring ten arrangement invoices and new centre hours to association
Trial licensed cleanup tool on own oboe takes and check notes manually
Require written player consent; stop for invented or missing notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the centre to put any cut in paid arrangement and rehearsal-note hours on paper. I would show the figures to the players and discuss the new fee with our association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a third of my pay comes from arranging short pieces and preparing section notes. I expect software to take those hours early; with two weeks saved, a third-pay gap is a mortgage problem immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten paid arrangement invoices with the centre's new schedule and bring them to the association. In the first year of change, I'll trial a new AI audio-cleanup tool on my own oboe takes only if its licence permits paid use, then compare each repaired note with the original before sending a client anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the likely fee cut is large and the reserve is tiny. I can learn a tool quickly. Fast audio cleanup does not restore my paid arranging hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose recording could enter that trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will not upload a pupil's lesson or another player's take without written permission. If the tool invents a note or removes someone's line, I will stop and use the original recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the association to seek a minimum preparation fee and a named person to sign off on recording reuse. I will bring the invoices rather than pretend every player has the same contract.

say: I'd ask for **written live calls** before AGI removes arranging income.
I'd tell players **robot oboists** follow thinking AGI by about three years.
think: **AGI in 2028** could erase arrangement fees before robots play around 2031.
Our **two-week reserve** cannot carry a third-pay loss while local vacancies are scarce.
do: List **three income streams** and request written paid calls now.
Apply **after 2028** if arrangements halve, only for a posted qualifying teacher role with pickup and written replacement net pay.
Keep **current pupils and orchestra** until offer; ask lender about total added interest before arrears if rehearsals fall.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a large loss may outrun savings and local job options.
S2.quote: A good solo audition is not a vacancy if no school can pay a teacher.
fieldNote: Her **2028 screen-work risk** precedes robot oboe playing around 2031.
Her **job move** requires a real post, recognised master's, child pickup and written net pay after travel.

steps.text: Keep orchestra/pupils until signed offer; list income and request written live calls
Apply after 2028 if arrangements halve and posted teacher role accepts master's
Require pickup and written net pay after travel before leaving orchestra or pupils
Ask lender before arrears if rehearsals fall; review written total added interest before accepting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the woodwinds that AGI by 2028 could arrange the score before robots can play oboe around 2031. I would ask the centre for every paid live call in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking work could become cheap before the orchestra changes a chair. If a third of my low pay vanishes, two weeks saved and Luis's variable shifts will not carry the mortgage while I search among very few local posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll separate concert, lesson and arranging pay and ask for next season's paid calls in writing. In the first year after 2028, if arranging income halves, I'll apply for a posted woodwind-teacher role within travel range only if my master's qualifies, the hours allow child pickup and written net pay after travel replaces the loss. I will keep the orchestra and five pupils until another offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a big loss arriving before another wage. A good solo audition is not a vacancy if no school can pay a teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the woodwind-teacher job open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nearest school filled a music post last year. I'll ask about the next opening, but I cannot put that old advert in our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if live rehearsals are cut too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the centre also cuts a paid rehearsal, Luis and I will ask the lender about temporary terms before arrears. We will get the total added interest in writing before accepting them.

say: I'd seek a **paid small-group class** with a signed room.
I'd keep **children's recordings** private without written family permission.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens arrangements before robot players arrive around 2034.
**Ordinary software** may cut paid preparation before the class fills.
do: Offer a **Saturday clarinet group** only with signed room, insurance, eight prepayments covering pay and eight inspected centre loan instruments.
Defer and **refund families** if instruments fail; require separate cleaned mouthpieces, personal reeds and written family recording consent.
Continue **after 2031** only with eight renewals, safe instruments, paid room terms and assistant cover.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because fees may fall before a safely funded class is ready.
S3.quote: There is no spare cash to pay a hall from our mortgage account.
fieldNote: Her **eight-place gate** protects household cash and paid teaching time when a hall hire and instrument checks could fail.
She requires **inspected instruments**, personal reeds and written permission for children's recordings.

steps.text: Book hall only with signed room and insurance terms
Start only with eight prepayments covering hire and teaching plus eight inspected centre loan clarinets
Defer/refund failed instruments; require separate cleaned mouthpieces, personal reeds and written family recording consent
Continue after 2031 with eight renewals, signed room/pay/insurance terms, eight safe instruments and funded assistant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the town that five years could let us build paid small-group lessons, if they pay the tutor and supply a room. I would ask the arts centre for terms before inviting parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could do arrangements and notes, while robot players arrive around 2034. Ordinary tools might trim paid preparation sooner, so a live class must earn money during the warning years rather than rely on future demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll propose a separate Saturday clarinet group at the community hall only if the hall signs room and insurance terms, eight families prepay enough to cover hire and my time, and the arts centre agrees to lend eight inspected clarinets. By 2031 I'll repeat it only if fees cover an assistant; in the first year after AGI, I'll continue only if eight renew and the room, pay and instrument conditions still hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed that preparation fees could fall before a class fills. I can organise the work. There is no spare cash to pay a hall from our mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are there eight safe instruments for the class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has six safe clarinets and two that need checking. I will not ask parents to buy the missing instruments; if fewer than eight pass, I'll defer and refund any fees already collected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How will pupils share mouthpieces or recordings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A reed is the thin piece that vibrates when a player blows into the mouthpiece. Pupils will use their own reeds, and I will not share a child's playing online without written family permission. Each pupil will also have a separate cleaned mouthpiece.

say: I'd seek a **funded teaching credential** that district schools accept.
I'd ask for **published school pay** before leaving current calls.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I still need wages for the mortgage.
**Arrangement fees** may fall earlier, with robot players following around 2039.
do: Check **district acceptance** and grant; enrol only with covered fees and Luis covering childcare.
Build **two months' savings** from cleared extra teaching after essential bills by 2036.
Take a **posted school role** after 2036 only if certified, with written net pay after travel covering mortgage and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** because the longer runway does not repair today's thin reserve.
S4.quote: I will not call an unsigned school salary our safety net.
fieldNote: Her **master's and leadership** make teaching plausible only if the district accepts and funds the certificate.
Her **two-month target** uses cleared extra pupil fees after essential bills, not an assumed new class.

steps.text: Enrol only if district accepts certificate, grant covers fees and Luis covers childcare
Save cleared extra-teaching pay after mortgage, food and electricity toward two months
Take qualifying posted school role after 2036 with written net-after-travel pay covering mortgage and pickup
Keep orchestra and pupils until school salary and hours are signed; check travel and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger players that ten years is time to build a recognised teaching route, if the district funds it. I would ask schools what they actually pay rather than rely on a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 in 2036 with the mortgage still due; robot players may reach stages around 2039. Arrangement fees could fall long before that, so I need paid work now as well as a qualification later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the district whether my master's qualifies for its classroom-music certificate and whether a grant covers fees. I'll enrol only if a grant covers fees, Luis can cover the children's evenings and the district accepts the course, while keeping my paid pupils and orchestra calls. By 2036 I'll aim to save two months of expenses from cleared extra teaching fees after the mortgage, food and electricity are paid; in the first year after AGI, I'll take a posted school role only if the district certificate qualifies me and a written net offer after travel covers the mortgage and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, because the ten years help with study but not this month's bills. I will not call an unsigned school salary our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the district certificate actually accepted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The district office has not confirmed that the certificate counts. I would wait for written acceptance and grant terms before enrolling or paying a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would two months of savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The arts centre might offer another pupil group, but nobody has signed up. I would move money into savings only after those fees clear and our essential bills are paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because arrangement fees could vanish before I can replace them in a town with few openings. Signed calls, a posted qualifying teaching job and the lender's full terms if live pay falls would help us keep the mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays when an instrument fails halfway through a class. No family should buy a replacement clarinet because a hall skipped an instrument inspection.

headlineQuote: No family should buy a replacement clarinet because a hall skipped an instrument inspection.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old woodwind leader** with a music master's, partner, two children and a mortgage.
Despite **senior skill**, her pay is low, savings cover two weeks and few similar jobs are nearby.
She uses **AI daily** but tests new cleanup tools only on owned takes with manual checks and permission.
She seeks **paid teaching** with safe instruments while retaining current work until another salary is signed.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could remove arranging fees before a replacement vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed live calls**, a qualifying posted job and full lender terms would help protect the mortgage.
